title: Table 6 reprints Table 5
published: Table 6, "Effects of information on favoring minimum wage raise," prints [[the contents of Table 5]], every cell identical, under a column header reading [["Dependent variable: T2 Amount"]].
corrected: [[This edition prints the Table 6 models the deposited GC_Study_2_analysis.R fits]], on favor_T2_recode, which are the estimates Figure 1's "Study 2: T2 Favor" panel plots.
note: Table 6, "Effects of information on favoring minimum wage raise," prints the contents of Table 5 rather than its own. Every cell is identical to Table 5's, and the column header inside Table 6 reads "Dependent variable: T2 Amount" where the table is captioned for the Favor outcome. The text is correct and the table is not: the deposited `GC_Study_2_analysis.R` fits its Table 6 models on `favor_T2_recode`, and Figure 1's "Study 2: T2 Favor" panel plots the estimates below rather than the ones Table 6 prints. The sentence after the table on p. 1506, "With the exception of negative information among opponents, all these coefficients are statistically significant," is false twice of the table the page prints: among opponents positive information without covariates is 0.43 (p = 0.40), and negative information with covariates is –0.70 (p = 0.02). Of the corrected table it holds cell for cell. All twelve information coefficients are correctly signed, and the only two not significant at the 0.1 level are opponents' negative information, –0.02 (p = 0.95) without covariates and –0.13 (p = 0.49) with them. The correction makes the text true. The corrected table follows.

title: The Study 3 positive information estimate among opponents
published: Focusing on the covariate-adjusted models, we estimate that a one-unit increase in positive information causes an average increase in support for capital punishment of 0.015 scale points among proponents and [[0.068]] scale points among opponents, neither of which is statistically significant.
corrected: Focusing on the covariate-adjusted models, we estimate that a one-unit increase in positive information causes an average increase in support for capital punishment of 0.015 scale points among proponents and [[0.074]] scale points among opponents, neither of which is statistically significant.
note: The published sentence gives 0.068 for opponents. The specification the deposit fits, and which Table 8's fourth column reports, gives 0.074. Both round to the 0.07 that Table 8 prints, so the disagreement is visible only at the precision the text itself uses. Dropping race from the covariate set gives 0.086, so the published figure comes from neither specification.

title: The Study 3 negative information estimate among opponents
published: Negative information has a strong negative effect among proponents (–0.326, p < 0.01), and a weakly negative effect among opponents ([[–0.042]], p = [[0.43]]).
corrected: Negative information has a strong negative effect among proponents (–0.326, p < 0.01), and a weakly negative effect among opponents ([[–0.040]], p = [[0.46]]).
note: The published sentence gives –0.042 and p = 0.43. Table 8's own fourth column, and the deposited specification behind it, give –0.040 with p = 0.46. The estimate is not significant at any conventional level on either figure.

title: The Study 3 movement from Con Con to Pro Pro among opponents
published: These estimates imply that moving from the Con Con condition to the Pro Pro condition would cause proponents to move 2·0.015 + 2·0.326 = 0.682 scale points and opponents to move 2·[[0.068]] + 2·[[0.042]] = [[0.220]] scale points.
corrected: These estimates imply that moving from the Con Con condition to the Pro Pro condition would cause proponents to move 2·0.015 + 2·0.326 = 0.682 scale points and opponents to move 2·[[0.074]] + 2·[[0.040]] = [[0.228]] scale points.
note: The published sentence gives 2·0.068 + 2·0.042 = 0.220. The arithmetic is right and the two inputs are the ones corrected in entries 4 and 5, so the total moves with them. It is computed from the inputs as printed, as the published total was; from their unrounded values it is 0.227.

title: The significance threshold in the Table 2 note
note: Three stars mark the most significant cells, not the least. Table 3's note, on the facing page, states the same threshold correctly. The starred cells are unaffected: the three-star coefficients in these tables have p-values of 0.0007 and below.

title: Table 1's standard deviations
published: Table 1 prints [[the standard errors of the means]] in its two SD columns, [[(0.00)]] as their standard errors, and [[no condition label]] on its first row.
corrected: [[Table 1 as the corrigendum corrects it]]: the standard deviation of each outcome in each condition, with its bootstrapped standard error, and the first row labelled Control.
note: A corrigendum the authors published at *British Journal of Political Science* 50(4), 1517, doi 10.1017/S0007123419000024, corrects Table 1 for a coding error that made the standard deviations and their standard errors inaccurate, and this edition sets its table. The SD columns the page prints repeat the standard errors of the means beside them. The corrected T2 Attitude standard deviations run from 0.99 to 1.02, which bears out the text's "the standard deviations of the outcomes do not appear to vary by treatment condition and are very precisely estimated." The T2 Belief standard deviations do vary, and could not fail to: the outcome is binary, so its standard deviation follows its mean, and means of 0.62 under negative information and 0.72 under positive give standard deviations of 0.49 and 0.45, a difference 3.3 times its bootstrapped standard error. No estimate in the article uses these standard deviations.
